units.text: AP Biology, AP Chemistry and AP Physics C **meet two periods a day** — a structural rigour signal rather than a post-AP course.

The school publishes no comparison of its grading severity against local public schools, and no third party audits it. The quintile table and the mandatory-exam policy are the implicit answer; a direct inflation comparison is unpublished.

The office does not publish a guarantee that every application is formally reviewed before submission, a codified Early Decision / Early Action strategy, a stated test-optional position, or FAFSA/CSS Profile timelines beyond the general “Paying for College” programming.

Two levers work at once: the student builds a verifiable spike through nation-first diploma programmes and a required internship, and the Academic Profile makes the school’s disclosure do the vouching.

**Global Studies Diploma** — “the first of its kind in the country”. Begins in 9th grade, requires a world language through all four years, globally-focused coursework, cross-cultural experience, an individual portfolio, and a lengthy research paper in the capstone Global Leadership course. **375 graduates since 2007**, 23 in the Class of 2026 alone.

**Required 30-hour Senior Project internship** — a graduation requirement, so every graduate leaves with a documented experiential credential. Notably the school has *no* community-service requirement, deliberately.

The Entrepreneurial Studies Diploma is announced but its course requirements, capstone and internship structure are not published — inquiries are directed to an email address. Compare Global Studies, which publishes both requirements and a 375-graduate throughput.

**The Academic Profile as an instrument** — an unusually disclosive document, and that is the leverage. It volunteers a full per-subject AP distribution across 29 subjects, a quintile table with mean SAT and ACT per fifth, explicit AP-load norms, and the weighting formula with unweighted grades on the transcript. It converts a no-rank policy from a liability into context.

**Integrity signalling** — the school states it complies with the **NACAC Guide to Ethical Practice** and “reports all student behavioral probations, suspensions and expulsions through time of graduation” to any college that asks, backed by a student-run Honor Council of eight students, two per grade, plus two elected faculty members and a third appointed by the Head of School. Disclosure earns reader trust, and that credibility accrues to every applicant.

**Repeat pipelines, numbered rather than implied** — the Class of 2025 scholar was Providence Day’s **18th Morehead-Cain**, a decades-deep pipeline to North Carolina’s most selective merit award. Bolded institutions across the list function as the de facto pipeline map, and four of the five federal service academies appear.

**Two-way relationships and memberships** — NAIS, NCAIS, SAIS, ERB, NACAC, SACAC, **ACCIS** and the College Board, accredited by SAIS and SACS, plus Global Online Academy, and **81%** of Upper School faculty hold advanced degrees. ~150 reps hosted against 50+ campuses visited is a genuine two-way cadence, and a deep UK/Europe pipeline (Oxford, St Andrews, UCL, LSE, Trinity Dublin, Bocconi, Toronto) matches the Global Studies identity.

It is also the most analytically honest table the school prints: a 338-point SAT gap between the top and bottom fifths shows a large, academically heterogeneous class rather than a uniformly elite one.

The profile publishes the mean and the middle 50% only. The middle-50% endpoints ARE the 25th and 75th percentiles, so those columns are real school figures; the 10th, 50th and 90th are shown as “—” rather than modelled, because the school does not publish them.

All five quintiles are the school’s own published figures — nothing here is interpolated. Read the spread: 4.507 → 3.204 is a 1.303 weighted-GPA gap and 1454 → 1116 a 338-point SAT gap. Because AP adds a full point, a 4.017 middle fifth is not a straight-A unweighted transcript — part of it is honours and AP weight. Note the quintiles describe the Class of 2027 while the test scores above describe the Class of 2026 — different cohorts, so do not blend them.

This is a **consultative** model, not a structured learning-differences programme — there is no published LD track, resource room, or accommodations-course structure. On-site occupational therapy exists; speech-language services are not published.

The 383-institution list spans Williams, MIT and Harvard down through Catawba, Brevard, Lees-McRae, Pfeiffer and Central Piedmont Community College — and crucially many accessible options are **bolded** as enrolling: App State, East Carolina, UNC–Charlotte, UNC–Greensboro, Western Carolina, High Point, Wingate, Gardner-Webb, Belmont Abbey and Central Piedmont. The fourth and fifth quintiles are genuinely being placed, not just listed.

Conservatories (Berklee, RISD, Parsons, SAIC, SCAD, School of Visual Arts, UNCSA), four of the five federal service academies, and a deep international roster (Oxford, St Andrews, Edinburgh, UCL, LSE, King’s College London, Trinity Dublin, Leiden, Amsterdam, Bocconi, Toronto).

No breakdown of outcomes BY quintile is published — the table gives inputs (GPA, SAT, ACT per fifth) but never says where the middle and bottom fifths actually enroll. That is the single biggest gap in an otherwise unusually disclosive profile.

1,282 exams at 93% scoring 3+ and 76% at 4–5, and 94% of the 497 students who sat them earned a 3 or higher — with the complete per-subject distribution printed, weak spots included. Because the exam is mandatory, those figures rest on a non-self-selected denominator.

The profile also carries an unusually candid warning about its own maths placement, and a spring-2026 decision to weight Advanced maths and science courses +0.5, applied retroactively from the Class of 2027.

**Honors Java Data Structures** sits beyond AP CS A, and **AP Cybersecurity** and **AP Networking Fundamentals** are now listed as two separate APs — both very new College Board offerings and a real differentiator.
Interdisciplinary

A weighted 4-point scale (A+ 4.33, A 4.00 for 93–97, down to F 0.00) giving **one additional quality point** for Honors and AP and **one-half point for each Advanced course** except Advanced Functions with Trigonometry. The scale was absent from every edition after 2017–18 and **returned in 2026–27**.
Four graduating classes produced acceptances at 337 institutions; 132 carry the newest list’s matriculation asterisk — at least one Latin student enrolled there in 2024–26.

The striking number is breadth: 61 of the 68 Power Four universities appear, the absences being Minnesota, Nebraska, BYU, UCF, Houston, Kansas State and UT Austin (the lists write only “University of Texas”), and seven of the eight Ivies — Columbia is the only one missing.
carry the 2024–26 matriculation asterisk

The merit-dollar total stopped being published after the Class of 2023 — the 2024, 2025 and 2026 write-ups carry no figure, and whether the school stopped collecting or stopped publishing it is unclear. Morehead-Cain attaches to the Class of 2022, outside this list’s window. QuestBridge, Robertson, Jefferson, Belk, Stamps and Coca-Cola were not found for any recent class; Robertson, Jefferson and Belk are attested only in a 2017–18 historical paragraph and should not be read as current pipelines. The 2026–27 profile carries no merit figures either.

Latin’s differentiators are narrow, deep and genuinely elite in two places — a top-20 national debate programme and an MIT-lineage Fab Lab — and the school leaves the assembly of a spike almost entirely to the student.

**Innovation & Design / Fab Lab** — an official Fab Lab school in the lineage of **MIT’s Center for Bits and Atoms**, and an active Fab Academy node since 2016. Engineering has been taught here since 1989; the lab runs 3D printing, CNC milling, circuit production, laser and precision milling. Upper School courses are taught “like a professional software engineering firm”, with students presenting to external panels of industry experts.

**Internships do exist**, contrary to a common assumption: a **Biomedical Internship Program** placing seniors with Atrium Health is course-embedded in Advanced Topics in Engineering, alongside a Student Internship Program elective.

There is still no required internship, capstone, senior project, independent study or school-wide research requirement — graduation requirements are purely credit-based, and there is no global-studies certificate or diploma. Athletic recruiting and arts-in-college support are informational programmes only: no named recruiting coordinator, highlight-film service, conservatory-prep track or portfolio review is published.

**The School Profile argues with numbers again.** It is the one document every admissions office reads, and the 2026–27 edition restores the grading scale, the weighting statement and the class-rank policy, and adds AP results and SAT and ACT means after years without them. It still omits a CEEB code, a four-year matriculation percentage and National Merit Finalists.

**Named-scholarship history was deleted too.** The 2017–18 edition told readers the school’s students had won Morehead-Cain, Robertson, B.N. Duke, Jefferson, Belk, Bryan, Chancellor’s, Danforth and Johnson scholarships, and gave application and matriculation breadth. Not one of those sentences survives, and the 2026–27 edition does not restore them.
**What remains is genuine and external** — the NSDA recognition, the Fab Academy node, and the Malone Family Foundation selection are all third-party validations that do not depend on the profile.

The figures are means, not distributions. A reader can now place a test score against the class average, but not against the spread — there is no middle-50% band and no share of the class above any line.

Verbatim: in the Upper School the programme “becomes more of a **consultative and coaching model**”, working on executive functioning — organisation, time management, study strategies. Lower School LR is explicitly remedial; the Upper School is not. Decisive for a family whose 9–12 student needs direct intervention.

Middle and Upper School students who qualify have a **504 Educational Plan**, with testing current within three years; typical accommodations include extended time and testing in a separate setting. Critically, **charges for sessions are not included in tuition and are billed per session each month**.

The Office of Academic Transition and Student Success is a **transition and belonging office** for students new to independent schools, particularly from underrepresented backgrounds. Its page never mentions learning differences, 504 plans or accommodations. A student with dyslexia who is neither new to Latin nor from an underrepresented background falls outside its stated population entirely.

In the Class of 2027’s junior year, 524 of 833 course grades (63%) were in the A range, and 457 of 806 (57%) in sophomore year — as counted from the profile’s own tables, which omit grades below C−. Beyond grades, the 337-institution list is genuinely broad, spanning Harvard, MIT and Stanford through Belhaven, Brevard, Catawba, Carson-Newman, Lenoir-Rhyne, Methodist, Saint Leo, Trevecca Nazarene, Wingate and Johnson & Wales, many carrying matriculation asterisks.

Nine UNC-system campuses carry a 2024–26 matriculation asterisk — Chapel Hill, NC State, Charlotte, Greensboro, Wilmington, Asheville, the School of the Arts, East Carolina and Appalachian State — so Latin visibly places students across the band rather than only at the top.

Service academies (the Naval Academy and The Citadel, plus a 2025 Air Force Academy appointment), conservatory and arts institutions, and international universities including St Andrews, UCL, King’s, Imperial, Leiden, Amsterdam, Queensland, Toronto, McGill and UBC all appear on the lists.
337 institutions across four classes with 61 of the 68 Power Four universities represented, and matriculation asterisks spread from the Ivies down through the regional band.

Because the exams are mandatory, the profile’s published exam, student and AP Scholar counts describe the whole AP cohort rather than its most confident testers. Four credits of Biblical Studies are the transcript’s defining signature.

All three National Merit figures are rolling 15-year windows, which is why the Finalist count can fall from 16 to 14 to 12 while Commended moves from 45 to 48 to 46 — strong older years drop out of the window. That is arithmetically possible rather than an error, but the school does not explain it, and no per-class-year ledger is published in any edition.

**Calculus III** is genuine post-AP depth — multivariable and vector-valued functions, curvature, double and triple integrals, vector analysis and differential equations. It requires a 93% in AP Calculus AB or completion of BC.

Graduation requires **27 credits including 4 of Biblical Studies**, plus a January Term credit, a half-credit Junior Seminar and a half-credit Speech course. Those four credits consume elective space peer schools spend elsewhere, and they are the transcript’s most distinctive feature.

Only the 3+ threshold is reported — the share of exams scoring 4 or 5 is not published in any year, so no 4–5 rate should be inferred. The 2026–27 profile also drops the pass count and the AP Scholar breakdown by award level that the 2024–25 edition printed. “Most rigorous” course-load norms are likewise undefined: there is no published rubric and no statement of what fraction of students take the most demanding programme.

No counselor tenure, prior employer or professional background is published for anyone on the team, and no bios appear on the college counseling page. Neither rep-visit counts nor counselor campus-visit counts are published.

**Academic Conservatory** — the school’s strongest published credential, and critically it is **noted on the transcript**, so it reaches the admissions reader rather than living only in a résumé. The 2026–27 profile names six areas — Math and Science; Fine Arts; Bible, Philosophy & Religion; English; Social Studies; World Languages — and **20% of the Class of 2026** earned at least one distinction.

**Winterim / January Term** — a required credit every year (0.25 per year toward graduation), supplying internships, travel and vocational shadowing. Note the vocational shadowing component is small: only about seven placements are published.

**Seal of Biliteracy** — implemented in 2019 and awarded on a proficiency exam across two languages, though the share earning it fell from 11% of the Class of 2021 to 4% of the Class of 2024, then rose to 7% of the Class of 2026.

**A Christian-college network with its own membership** — Charlotte Christian belongs to **NACCAP**, the Christian-college counseling association, alongside NACAC and SACAC. Its brochure gives Christian colleges a named tier, and 14% of graduates enroll at one. Class of 2026 graduates enrolled at Wheaton, Liberty, Samford, Gordon, Lipscomb and Baylor.

**The School Profile as an instrument** — it publishes the AP exam, student and AP Scholar counts, a five-quintile GPA table, a GPA middle 50% (3.604–4.199 for the Class of 2026), the grading scale and the weighting formula, plus CEEB 340667.

**Granular scholarship reporting** — roughly ninety individually named awards published for a single class is far more specific than a headline dollar figure, and lets a family see which institutions actually fund this school’s students.

The disciplinary policy is published: the school follows the NACAC Statement of Principles of Good Practice and “does not permit the reporting of any disciplinary infractions”, but it advises students to self-disclose any grade 9–12 infraction that led to an out-of-school suspension.

The median student sits in the third quintile at roughly 3.80–4.05 weighted, and the profile puts the class’s GPA middle 50% at 3.604–4.199 on its GPA scale. Because Honors adds 0.5 and AP a full point, a 4.240 top-quintile floor implies a heavy advanced load rather than a perfect record.

All five quintiles are the school’s own published figures. Against the Class of 2025 table, the distribution compressed in one year: the first-quintile floor eased from 4.277 to 4.240, while the third rose from 3.686 to 3.804, the fourth from 3.124 to 3.542 and the fifth from 1.941 to 2.269. The bottom of the class moved up much more than the top moved down. No unweighted distribution is published.

Two Upper School counselors provide study-skills instruction, course-selection guidance, academic progress monitoring, test-anxiety management, and referrals to outside resources. That is a general counseling function rather than a learning-differences programme.

**WIN (“What I Need”) labs** and advisory lessons are the named Upper School academic-support structure, and the **Media & Writing Center** is free and writing-specific. What WIN Lab delivers academically is not described.
The middle may be the best-served cohort

The list spans Duke, Harvard and Columbia down to Central Piedmont Community College, Barton, Catawba, Spartanburg Methodist, Belmont Abbey, Wingate and Winthrop. A fourth- or fifth-quintile student at 3.54 or below has real, named destinations, and the checklist instructs students to include “every possible type of college that might be of interest”.

A structurally rigorous, transparent transcript — mandatory AP exams, a full published quintile table, published AP exam and Scholar counts — attached to the thinnest learning-support disclosure in this set.
the 2026–27 profile prints 435 exams, 208 students and 90 AP Scholars beside the 94%, so the rate can be read against the size of the cohort that earned it.

A biblical-worldview college-prep school that does not rank; the transcript rests on a weighted GPA with an honors and AP quality-point bonus, and an AP catalog that reaches AP Seminar and AP Research.

The school advertises **17 AP courses plus AP Capstone** (AP Seminar + AP Research). The 2026–27 profile names 13 by title (Calculus BC and Psychology are no longer printed; Human Geography is back); the 2023 profile named 17, which cover every title any edition has printed, so which of them run in a given year varies.

Courses taught on campus are credited through **Judson College** (2026–27 profile; prior years credited via the College at Southeastern), and only courses taught by HGCS teachers carry dual credit; students also take **NC Career & College Promise** courses at local community colleges.

The seniors-per-counselor ratio is not published; against the Class of 2025 senior count, the latest the school has published, it computes to roughly 34:1 across the two staff, or about 144:1 measured over all 287 high-school students.

The guidance page describes these as its program rather than publishing a grade-by-grade timeline. No application-platform account (Naviance / SCOIR / Common App) and no NCAA code are stated on any of the profiles or the guidance page.

158 distinct institutions appear across the school's three published acceptance lists (Classes of 2023, 2025 and 2026) — from Bowdoin, Pomona, Georgia Tech and Boston University through a deep bench of NC publics, Christian colleges and HBCUs.
The lists carry no matriculation markings, so they read as acceptances, and no Class of 2024 list was published. Here the combined, deduplicated list is scored against the current U.S. News tiers.
158 institutions across three published class lists · no matriculation markings
No per-college matriculation markings — acceptances only
**A legible, no-rank transcript** — the school does not rank, and publishes both grading scales and the honors/AP weighting so a reader can reconstruct rigor in context.

Fee-based **Educational Support Services (ESS)**, under an annual contract, serve K through 12th grade: accommodations plans built from educational testing or a prior 504/IEP, approved testing accommodations, and high school Academic Coaching.

The three acceptance lists run from Bowdoin, Pomona, Georgia Tech and Boston University through the full NC public system (Chapel Hill, NC State, Charlotte, Wilmington, Greensboro, Asheville, Pembroke), Christian colleges, HBCUs and community colleges (Central Piedmont, Cape Fear, Rowan-Cabarrus) — the spread of a broad, not uniformly elite, class.

The 2026–27 profile puts typical post-high-school plans at 65% 4-year college, 25% 2-year college and 10% work, military or a gap year. The Class of 2025, the last year printed with counts, had 22% planning a 2-year college and 11% choosing not to pursue higher education — and the acceptance list includes the community colleges and trade paths that reflects.

No score percentiles, no GPA quintiles and no per-quintile outcomes are published — only class means/medians (with disclosed tester counts) and AP awardee tiers. The shape of the class is not recoverable from public sources.

A biblical-worldview college-prep school with a genuine AP-and-Capstone program and a widening recognition record — with the small tester counts and the unpublished caseload the two things a visit should probe.
17 AP courses with AP Capstone, 176 exams sat in May 2026, 14 students earning a 5 on at least one, and 3 AP Capstone Diplomas — a program with genuine depth for a school this size.

158 institutions across the 2023, 2025 and 2026 lists — Bowdoin and Pomona at the top, 23 HBCUs, the full NC public system — but the lists mark no matriculations, so they show acceptances, not enrollment.
The school publishes class means on small tester counts (SAT n=45), not percentile distributions or a GPA table, and does not rank — so the shape of the class is not public.
The acceptance lists mark no enrollments — where did the Classes of 2024, 2025 and 2026 actually matriculate, and in what concentrations?
